subject: Mathematics
title: Amir's Mango Market Data Adventure
hook: Learn to read and create pictographs and bar graphs using a real village fruit market.

characters.name: Amir
characters.role: the fruit vendor's son learning to count sales

characters.name: Neha
characters.role: Amir's friend who loves puzzles and patterns

characters.name: Mr. Verma
characters.role: the market vendor who teaches data collection

slides.title: Data Through Pictures
slides.storyContext: Amir's father owns a fruit stall in the village market. Every day, he sells mangoes, bananas, oranges, and apples. But he never remembers which fruit sells best! Neha suggests: 'Let's collect data and show it with pictures. Then you'll know at a glance!'
slides.inSimpleWords: Data is information we collect. Pictures help us understand data quickly.

image.alt: Data Through Pictures — Data Through Pictures

slides.title: Collecting Fruit Sales Data
slides.storyContext: For one week, Amir and Neha keep a tally. Every time someone buys mangoes, they draw one dot. Bananas get a mark, oranges get a mark, apples get a mark. By Sunday, they have hundreds of marks! Mr. Verma, the elderly shop owner next door, watches them and says, 'You're doing what shops call data collection. Now organize it so we can see the real story.'
slides.inSimpleWords: We collect data by counting or recording things. A tally mark or tally table helps us keep track.

slides.title: Tally Marks: Counting Made Easy
slides.storyContext: Neha shows Amir the tally method. 'Every line is one item. But at five, we cross the diagonal line through four others, making a group of five. Then we count faster!' They organize their fruit sales: Mangoes ⊢⊣⊢ (13), Bananas ⊢⊣⊢⊣ (19), Oranges ⊢⊣ (8), Apples ⊢⊣⊢⊣⊢⊣ (25).

points.label: Tally Mark
points.text: A single line (|) representing one count

points.label: Grouped Tally
points.text: Four vertical lines crossed by a diagonal line (⊢⊣) represents 5 items

points.label: Counting Tallies
points.text: Count groups of 5, then add remaining individual marks

points.label: Why tallies?
points.text: Easier than writing numbers, and grouped marks help us count faster

example.problem: Amir makes these tallies for Saturday sales: Mangoes ⊢⊣⊢| (11 marks). How many mangoes were sold?

slides.inSimpleWords: Tally marks help us count quickly. Groups of 5 (crossed line) make counting easier.

slides.title: Pictographs: Using Pictures to Show Data
slides.storyContext: Neha says, 'What if instead of numbers, we draw little pictures?' She draws a small mango symbol 🥭 for each item sold. But since 25 apples is too many drawings, Mr. Verma suggests: 'One big apple picture can mean 5 apples sold. That way, we use fewer pictures but still show the same data!'

points.label: Pictograph
points.text: A graph using small pictures or symbols instead of numbers

points.label: Picture Symbol
points.text: Represents one or more items (e.g., one 🥭 = 1 mango, or one 🍎 = 5 apples)

points.label: Key/Scale
points.text: Shows what each picture means (e.g., '1 picture = 5 items')

points.label: Partial pictures
points.text: Half a picture means half the value (e.g., half of 5 apples = 2.5 apples)

example.problem: A pictograph shows oranges sold using 🍊 symbols. The key says 1 🍊 = 3 oranges. If there are 3 full symbols and 1 half symbol, how many oranges were sold?

slides.inSimpleWords: A pictograph uses pictures to show data. Each picture can mean 1 item or many items, based on the key.

slides.title: Bar Graphs: Data in Columns
slides.storyContext: Mr. Verma pulls out a chart drawn on grid paper. 'This is a bar graph. Each fruit gets a column, and the height of the column shows how many sold.' Amir sees vertical bars for each fruit. Bananas have the tallest bar (19), so they sold best. Oranges have the shortest bar (8). 'So bananas are our winner!' exclaims Neha.

points.label: Bar Graph
points.text: Uses vertical (or horizontal) bars to compare quantities

points.label: Axis Labels
points.text: X-axis (horizontal) shows categories (mangoes, bananas, etc.), Y-axis (vertical) shows the count

points.label: Bar Height/Length
points.text: Represents the value for each category; taller/longer bar = larger quantity

points.label: Reading Bars
points.text: Look at where the top of each bar aligns with the scale on the Y-axis

example.problem: A bar graph shows fruit sales: Mangoes bar reaches 13, Bananas bar reaches 19, Oranges bar reaches 8, Apples bar reaches 25. Which fruit was the most sold? Which was the least sold?
example.solution: Most sold: Apples (25). Least sold: Oranges (8).

slides.inSimpleWords: A bar graph uses tall or short bars to compare numbers. Taller bar = bigger number.

slides.title: Creating Your Own Bar Graph
slides.storyContext: Amir decides to make his own bar graph on grid paper. He writes the fruit names along the bottom (X-axis) and numbers (0–30) along the side (Y-axis). For each fruit, he colors in squares from the bottom up to the number sold. Neha checks his work: 'Perfect! Now anyone can see that bananas and apples are our bestsellers.'

points.label: Step 1: Draw Axes
points.text: Draw a horizontal line (X-axis) and vertical line (Y-axis)

points.label: Step 2: Label Axes
points.text: X-axis gets categories (fruit names); Y-axis gets numbers (count scale)

points.label: Step 3: Draw Bars
points.text: For each category, draw a bar reaching up to the correct number

points.label: Step 4: Color/Shade
points.text: Fill or color the bars so they stand out; add a title

example.problem: You have data: Apples 12, Bananas 18, Grapes 10, Oranges 15. Create a bar graph with X-axis labeled with fruit names and Y-axis numbered 0–20.
example.solution: Draw four bars: Apples bar to 12, Bananas bar to 18, Grapes bar to 10, Oranges bar to 15. Ensure each bar's top aligns with its number on the Y-axis.

slides.inSimpleWords: Making a bar graph: draw two lines (axes), label them, then draw bars for each category up to its number.

slides.title: Comparing and Interpreting Graphs
slides.storyContext: Amir's father looks at the bar graph and says, 'So we sold 25 apples and 19 bananas, but only 8 oranges. That means people prefer apples and bananas. Maybe I should buy more apple trees!' Neha adds, 'And we know exactly how much more: 25 − 8 = 17 more apples than oranges.'

points.label: Comparison
points.text: Bar graphs let us compare quantities at a glance (which is biggest, smallest, equal)

points.label: Finding Differences
points.text: Subtract one value from another (e.g., 25 − 8 = 17 more apples than oranges)

points.label: Finding Totals
points.text: Add all bars together to find total sales (e.g., 13 + 19 + 8 + 25 = 65 total fruits)

points.label: Making Decisions
points.text: Data guides real-world choices (stock more of bestsellers, less of slow items)

example.problem: Bar graph shows: Monday 12 customers, Tuesday 18 customers, Wednesday 10 customers, Thursday 15 customers. How many more customers came on Tuesday than Wednesday? What was the total for the week so far?
example.solution: Tuesday − Wednesday = 18 − 10 = 8 more customers on Tuesday. Total = 12 + 18 + 10 + 15 = 55 customers.

slides.inSimpleWords: Graphs help us compare and make real decisions. We can see which is biggest, find differences, and add totals.

slides.title: A Week of Market Data: The Full Story
slides.storyContext: Amir and Neha collect data for an entire week and present it to Mr. Verma. They create both a pictograph and a bar graph. Mr. Verma studies them carefully and says, 'Excellent work! Now I see the real story of my market. Let's use this to plan next month.'

example.problem: Weekly fruit sales: Mon (M=5, B=7, O=3, A=8), Tue (M=6, B=9, O=4, A=10), Wed (M=4, B=5, O=2, A=6), Thu (M=7, B=10, O=5, A=12), Fri (M=8, B=12, O=6, A=14). Create a pictograph using symbols where 1 symbol = 2 fruits. Also, calculate total apples sold for the week.
example.solution: Monday total: 5+7+3+8 = 23 fruits. Tuesday total: 6+9+4+10 = 29 fruits. Wednesday total: 4+5+2+6 = 17 fruits. Thursday total: 7+10+5+12 = 34 fruits. Friday total: 8+12+6+14 = 40 fruits. Total apples for week: 8+10+6+12+14 = 50 apples. Pictograph: Each day gets symbols for each fruit type, with each symbol representing 2 fruits.

slides.inSimpleWords: Real data from a week tells a big story. Both pictographs and bar graphs help us see patterns and trends.

image.alt: A Week of Market Data: The Full Story — Data Through Pictures

slides.title: Mystery: Which Fruit Wins?
slides.storyContext: Neha challenges Amir: 'I've made a bar graph of sales for the last 10 days, but I mixed up the labels! Bananas, Oranges, Apples, and Mangoes are jumbled. The bar heights are 10, 18, 12, and 25. Can you figure out which fruit is which based on what we know sells best?'

example.problem: Four bars show: 10, 18, 12, and 25. Based on the previous week's data (Apples were highest, Oranges were lowest), assign fruit names to each bar.
example.solution: Most likely: Apples = 25 (highest), Bananas = 18, Mangoes = 12, Oranges = 10 (lowest). This matches the pattern from last week where apples were popular and oranges sold the least.

slides.inSimpleWords: Sometimes we need to use patterns and logic to read graphs, not just the numbers.

slides.title: The Market Data Story
slides.storyContext: At the end of the week, Amir's father thanks both children. 'You've taught me to see my business through data. I now know exactly which fruits to stock and which to reduce. That's the power of data!' Neha smiles: 'And it all started with simple pictures and bars.'

points.label: Tally Marks
points.text: Help us count data quickly using groups of 5

points.label: Pictographs
points.text: Use pictures and symbols to show data; each picture has a fixed value

points.label: Bar Graphs
points.text: Use vertical or horizontal bars to compare quantities

points.label: Interpreting Data
points.text: We can compare (bigger, smaller), find differences, and make real decisions based on graphs

points.label: Data in Real Life
points.text: Markets, schools, hospitals use graphs to make smart choices

slides.inSimpleWords: Graphs turn numbers into pictures. Pictures make it easy to understand data and make good decisions.

subject: The World Around Us
title: Ravi and Priya Explore Their School
hook: Two friends discover how a school brings everyone together to learn and grow.

slides.title: Our School - A Happy Place
slides.storyContext: Ravi and Priya walk into their school on the first day of the term.

slides.title: Welcome to School!
slides.storyContext: Ravi and Priya feel a mix of excitement and nervousness. Mr. Sharma greets them at the gate with a warm smile. 'Come, let me show you around,' he says. 'Our school is like a big family where everyone learns, plays, and grows together.'

slides.title: What is a School?
slides.storyContext: As they walk through the hallways, Mr. Sharma explains: 'A school is a place where students come to learn new things.'

points.text: A school is a building where children gather to study and learn.
Teachers guide students in understanding subjects like Mathematics, Science, and English.
Schools have classrooms, libraries, playgrounds, and other facilities.

slides.inSimpleWords: A school is a special place where we learn important things and make friends.

slides.title: Different Roles in School
slides.storyContext: Priya asks, 'Who are all these people here?' Mr. Sharma points around: 'Everyone has an important job.'

points.label: Teachers
points.text: Help students learn subjects and solve problems.

points.label: Principal
points.text: Leads the school and makes sure everything runs smoothly.

points.label: Librarian
points.text: Takes care of books and helps students find information.

points.label: Helpers/Support Staff
points.text: Keep the school clean and safe.

slides.inSimpleWords: Every person in school—teachers, principal, helpers—works together to make it a good place for learning.

slides.title: School Rules and Routines
slides.storyContext: As the bell rings at 9 a.m., Ravi notices everyone moves to their classrooms. 'We follow routines,' Mr. Sharma says, 'so learning happens smoothly for everyone.'

points.text: School starts and ends at set times.
We follow rules: listening in class, raising hands to speak, being on time.
There are times for lessons, breaks, lunch, and play.
Rules keep everyone safe and happy.

slides.inSimpleWords: Schools have rules and a daily schedule so everyone knows what to do and when.

slides.title: Learning Subjects and Skills
slides.storyContext: Priya peeks into a classroom where students are solving math problems. 'What subjects do we study?' she asks. Mr. Sharma smiles: 'Many important ones!'

points.label: Mathematics
points.text: Numbers, shapes, and problem-solving.

points.label: Science
points.text: Understanding animals, plants, weather, and how things work.

points.label: English/Languages
points.text: Reading, writing, and speaking clearly.

points.label: Social Studies
points.text: Learning about people, places, history, and geography.

slides.inSimpleWords: In school, we study many subjects to learn about the world and become smart and curious.

slides.title: The School Playground
slides.storyContext: At noon, Ravi and Priya run to the playground. Children play cricket, badminton, and games. 'This is where we grow stronger,' Ravi says happily.

points.text: Playgrounds have space for games and sports.
Playing makes our bodies strong and healthy.
Games teach teamwork, fairness, and following rules.
Play time is just as important as study time.

slides.inSimpleWords: A school playground is where we play games, exercise, and have fun while becoming healthier.

slides.title: Library - The House of Books
slides.storyContext: Next, they visit the library. Rows of colorful books line the shelves. The librarian shows them how to borrow books. 'Here, you can find stories, knowledge, and adventure,' she says.

points.text: A library has many books on different topics.
We can borrow books to read at home and return them later.
Libraries help us learn beyond textbooks.
Quiet and peaceful reading space is important in a library.

slides.inSimpleWords: A library is like a treasure chest of books that help us explore new ideas and stories.

slides.title: A Day in School
slides.storyContext: Mr. Sharma gives them a schedule: '8:45 a.m.—arrive at school. 9:00 a.m.—morning assembly and flag hoisting. 10:00 a.m.—English class. 11:00 a.m.—break (15 min). 11:15 a.m.—Math class. 12:15 p.m.—Science. 1:15 p.m.—lunch. 2:00 p.m.—sports. 3:00 p.m.—art and crafts. 3:30 p.m.—assembly and dismissal.'

example.problem: If Ravi's English class starts at 9:00 a.m. and lasts 1 hour, what time does it end?
example.solution: 9:00 a.m. + 1 hour = 10:00 a.m. English class ends at 10:00 a.m.

slides.title: Your School Challenge
slides.storyContext: Now it's time for Ravi and Priya to think: 'How can we be good students and make our school happier?'

example.problem: Write three ways you can help make your school a happy place.
example.solution: 1. Listen to teachers and follow rules. 2. Be kind to friends and help others. 3. Keep the school clean and take care of books and materials.

slides.title: What We Learned
slides.storyContext: As they leave school that day, Ravi and Priya feel excited about coming back tomorrow.

points.text: A school is a place for learning, playing, and growing.
Teachers, principal, helpers, and librarians all help run the school.
School has rules, routines, and subjects we study.
Playgrounds and libraries are important parts of a school.
Every student can help make the school happy and safe.

slides.inSimpleWords: School is our learning home where friends and teachers help us grow into thoughtful, smart people.

subject: The World Around Us
title: Ravi and Priya Discover India
hook: Two friends explore India's diverse cultures, languages, festivals, and people across many states.

slides.title: Our Vibrant Country
slides.storyContext: Ravi and Priya visit their grandmother's house and ask her stories about India.

slides.title: The Land of Diversity
slides.storyContext: Grandma spreads a big map of India on the floor. 'Look, this is our country,' she says. 'From north to south, east to west, we have so many different people, languages, foods, and festivals. That's what makes India special—unity in diversity.'

slides.title: India - Our Country
slides.storyContext: Priya traces the outline: 'How big is India?' Grandma smiles: 'India is a large country in South Asia with 28 states and 8 union territories.'

points.text: India is the world's largest democracy.
Its capital city is New Delhi.
India is surrounded by oceans: the Arabian Sea, Bay of Bengal, and Indian Ocean.
The Himalayan Mountains are in the north.

slides.inSimpleWords: India is a big, beautiful country where many different people, religions, and languages live together in peace.

slides.title: States and Union Territories
slides.storyContext: 'How many states are there?' Ravi asks. Grandma points to different regions: 'Each state has its own capital, government, and special features.'

points.text: India has 28 states and 8 union territories.
Each state has its own capital city.
Major states include Maharashtra, Karnataka, Tamil Nadu, Gujarat, and West Bengal.
Union territories include Delhi, Goa, and Andaman & Nicobar Islands.

slides.inSimpleWords: India is divided into states and territories, each with its own government and special identity.

slides.title: Languages of India
slides.storyContext: Ravi hears Grandma sing in Tamil, then speak Hindi, then English. 'How many languages does one person need to know?' Priya laughs.

points.text: India has 22 official languages recognized by the Constitution.
Hindi is spoken most widely in the north; Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, and Malayalam in the south.
English is widely used for business and education.
Hundreds of dialects and local languages are also spoken.

slides.inSimpleWords: India celebrates many languages—each state has its own language, yet people understand each other through respect and learning.

slides.title: Religions and Beliefs
slides.storyContext: Grandma tells them: 'Our country is home to people of many faiths. Some follow Hinduism, some Islam, Christianity, Sikhism, Buddhism, and Jainism. All are equal and respected.'

points.text: Hinduism is practiced by the majority of Indians.
Islam, Christianity, Sikhism, Buddhism, and Jainism also have millions of followers in India.
Our Constitution guarantees freedom to practice any religion.
Respect for all religions is a core value of Indian society.

slides.inSimpleWords: Indians follow many different religions, and the country respects and protects everyone's beliefs.

slides.title: Indian Festivals
slides.storyContext: Ravi sees pictures of Diwali lights, Holi colors, Eid celebrations, Christmas decorations, and Durga Puja all around the room. 'We celebrate so many festivals!' he exclaims.

points.text: Diwali (Hindu Festival of Lights) brings families together with lamps and fireworks.
Holi (Festival of Colors) celebrates spring and the victory of good over evil.
Eid-ul-Fitr and Eid-ul-Adha are celebrated by Muslims with prayers and feasts.
Christmas, Pongal, and Durga Puja are celebrated with joy and community spirit.
Each festival has its own story, traditions, and special foods.

slides.inSimpleWords: Indians celebrate different festivals throughout the year, and each festival teaches us about culture, history, and values.

slides.title: People, Occupations, and Lifestyles
slides.storyContext: Grandma describes her village: 'Some people farm rice and wheat. In the cities, people work in offices, shops, hospitals, and schools. In mountains, people raise sheep and grow apples. On coasts, people fish.'

points.text: Many Indians work in farming—rice, wheat, sugar cane, and spices.
In cities, people work in offices, shops, factories, hospitals, and schools.
Coastal regions have fishing as a major occupation.
Artisans make textiles, pottery, handicrafts, and jewelry—skills passed through generations.
Different regions have different lifestyles based on geography and resources.

slides.inSimpleWords: India's people have different jobs and ways of living, but all work hard to build a strong, prosperous nation.

slides.title: Journey Across India
slides.storyContext: Grandma plans an imaginary trip: 'From Kashmir in the north with snow-capped mountains to Kerala in the south with coconut beaches. From Rajasthan's golden deserts to Assam's green tea gardens. We can travel 2,000+ kilometers and see completely different places, people, and foods.'

example.problem: If you travel from Delhi to Bangalore (about 2,150 km by road), and your car travels at 80 km per hour with a break, approximately how many hours will the journey take (not counting the break)?
example.solution: 2,150 km ÷ 80 km/hour ≈ 26.8 hours (about 27 hours of driving). With stops, a real journey takes 2-3 days.

slides.title: Discover Your State
slides.storyContext: Priya asks: 'Which state do you live in? What's special about it?'

example.problem: Research and write about your state: What is its capital? What language is spoken? What is one famous festival or feature?
example.solution: Example for Maharashtra: Capital is Mumbai. Marathi and Hindi are spoken. Diwali is a major festival, and we are known for Bollywood films, cotton farming, and the Taj Mahal (in Agra, nearby).

slides.title: What We Learned
slides.storyContext: As evening falls, Ravi and Priya hug Grandma. They realize India is truly a land of wonders.

points.text: India is a large, democratic country with 28 states and 8 union territories.
Indians speak many languages but understand each other with respect and effort.
Multiple religions are practiced, and all are equally respected.
Festivals like Diwali, Holi, and Eid bring communities together.
People across India have different occupations and lifestyles but share pride in being Indian.
Unity in diversity is India's greatest strength.

slides.inSimpleWords: India is one beautiful, diverse nation where people of different religions, languages, and backgrounds live as brothers and sisters.
